title.narrative: Voucher Program Mother and Child Health Phase III

description.narrative: During Phase III Yamaan propose to focus on Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) currently residing in key urban areas, hosted within the community and accessing already over-burdened urban facilities.For the last three years the war and conflict in Yemen has forced more than 2 million IDPs to flee their homes(7% of the Yemeni population), 89% of whom are displaced for more than a year1. This places a continued and prolonged burden on hosting families and the wider community, as well as on IDPs paying rent. It is estimated that 77% of the IDP population resides in private settings: host family, rented accommodation, or second home.2 Sana’a Capital, Amran and Ibb are main governorates hosting IDPs from other areas like Tiazz, Sa’ada and AlDhale. IDPs in Sana’a Capital mainly live in rented accommodation (89%) compared to those who live in host families (11%), while in Ibb the figures are 56% and 28%, respectively.In Phase I and II, the team worked with the assumption that people residing in urban areas are wealthy, hence targeted the voucher toward poorer rural areas. However, the current crisis in Yemen has left no area unaffected, with more pressure on urban areas due to internal displacement, especially in areas like Sana’a Capital and Ibb. A March 6th report by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) explained that the Yemenis are facing multiple crises, including armed conflict, displacement, risk of famine and the outbreaks of diseases including cholera — creating the world’s worst humanitarian crisis. Projected service resultsWith an overall target beneficiary population of 895,395 people (in Ibb and Sana’a Capital)of which 179,079 women at reproductive age are directly targeted, the programme will distribute 45,000 Safe Motherhood and 45,000 Family Planning vouchers over a period of 12 months (from January to December 2020). In that period, we expect the voucher programme to support about 22,500 deliveries, representing 50% of the overall deliveries expected in the target women. The voucher utilisation rate for deliveries is based on results from Phase II. Availability of essential commodities and lack of trained staff represent a major challenge for the achievement of Family Planning results. Already during Phase I a lack of personnel trained on long acting methods of contraception meant that women would have to use short term methods, not included in the programme’s benefit package

recipient-country.narrative: system is struggling to cope under the pressure of the continuing emergency. More than half of all health facilities are closed due to damage, destruction, or lack of funds. The largest cholera epidemic in the world is currently spreading across Yemen, exacerbated by deteriorating hygiene and sanitation conditions and disruptions to the water supply. 84 percent of Yemen’s estimated 2.9 million internally displaced persons have been displaced for over a year, resulting in additional needs due to depleted savings, lack of access to financial resources and the saturation of available housing capacity. Despite a decline since 1990, maternal mortality ratio (MMR) in Yemen remains among the highest in the region, at 385 deaths per 100,000 live births. The risk is significantly higher for marginalized and vulnerable groups: the MMR in rural areas is 69 percent higher than urban areas, and 80 percent of maternal deaths are among women and girls with less than primary education. The intervening two and a half years of conflict have worsened the situation considerably since these statistics were captured. Women and girls have fewer of the protective factors commonly available to men and boys to mitigate the impact of crisis and emergency: income, assets, access to health and education, social networks, political voice, legal protection and the realization of basic human rights. The incidence of gender-based violence also increases during conflict, with early/forced marriage becoming more common. These factors increase the likelihood of unintended pregnancy and the associated risk. Contraception and safe motherhood services are particularly important under these conditions to enable women to delay and space pregnancies and access vital medical assistance before, during and after childbirth. In 2013, only 45 percent of births were attended by skilled health staff and only 30 percent were in a health facility. 62 percent of women had a need for contraception but only 27 percent were using it. Given the deteriorating health facilities, lack of service providers and essential supplies, it is an even greater challenge for women to access services today. Many women and girls, particularly in rural areas, lack the funds to pay for transport and service costs associated with accessing the formal health system.
